name: Quaker Drab
lede: Quaker Drab is a warm, light brownish grey that Maerz and Paul traced back to 1802, among the oldest names in this corner of the library, and one that four different color systems have each tried to pin down since.

sections.title: Four systems, one grey
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives plate 46 B2 and dates the name to 1802 [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* lists a near match at plate LI, hue 1''''', read from a scan of an aged printed plate, so it is approximate [1]. The National Bureau of Standards folded both into ISCC-NBS block 265 in 1955, calling it a medium gray, and the industrial RAL system later assigned it an approximate equivalent, RAL 7048 [1].

Its exact hex, #858078, is shared with a second library name, [[pebble-grey|Pebble Grey]], one of the handful of cases in our library where two different names, from two different eras, land on precisely the same swatch [1]. A paler sibling, [[pale-quaker-drab|Pale Quaker Drab]] (#9E9A95), follows the same "Quaker" adjective toward a lighter grey, while [[quaker-blue|Quaker Blue]] carries the word into a much darker, bluer near-black [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of it covers at least 5 percent of the canvas in 1,292 of our 23,781 archive paintings, as photographed, more common than 86 percent of our named colors [2]. It most often plays a light tone, 36 percent of the 658 paintings where our within-painting lens finds it, and it peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 1.7 times the expected rate [2]. Shen Zhou is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 8 of his 12 works, 7.3 times what his era's baseline would predict [2]. The earliest dated painting is from 1200, 712 years before Ridgway's 1912 record, a floor set by thin early coverage rather than a true first sighting [2].
